title: Adaptive per-prefix TTL scheduling and cache-key shaping for cost-stable inference
creator: Arianna Patel
description: Background: Production telemetry shows substantial prefix skew: a small fraction of prefixes account for ~60% of cache hits while long-tail prefixes are cold and inflate per-token cost. Current static TTLs over-retain cold prefixes and under-serve hot prefixes, increasing both latency and spend. Goal: build a robust, production-safe system to (1) shape cache keys for prefix-family merging, (2) schedule per-prefix TTL ladders based on observed access sparsity, and (3) provide an automated but conservative rollout with clear rollback triggers to keep cost and latency SLOs stable. Success metrics: median token cost delta <= -10% (reduce cost by >=10%), 90th-pct latency change <= +5% during rollout, hit-rate uplift in hot cohorts >= +8%, zero customer-impact incidents during staged rollout.
motivation_and_context: We need a deterministic, auditable way to reduce unnecessary cache occupancy and improve effective hit-rate without exposing customers to regressions. This ticket focuses on the decisioning and safety workflow: how we derive per-prefix policies from telemetry, how we transform keys to reduce sparsity safely, and how we apply TTL schedules incrementally with fast rollback fences.
approach: 1) Offline modeling: build a sparsity-aware prefix exposure simulator that uses sampled production traces (1% reservoir samples over 7 days) to estimate hit curves for candidate key merges and TTL ladders. 2) Key shaping: implement a conservative fuzzy-merge normalizer that collapses variable user tokens (IDs, timestamps) using extraction heuristics and configurable token masks. 3) TTL laddering: for each prefix-family, compute a discrete set of TTL candidates (e.g., 30s, 60s, 300s) with expected hit elasticity and expected cost delta. 4) Safety envelopes: derive per-prefix confidence intervals via bootstrap and establish safe-change thresholds (min hit-rate change, max latency delta, max spend variance). 5) Rollout plan: shadow -> small canary (1% traffic) -> staged uplift (1%, 5%, 20%, 100%) with automated health checks and rollback triggers. 6) Observability: add per-prefix dashboards and an automatic regression alert that ties to the rollout pipeline.
experiments_and_results_summary: Prototype run on a subset of multi-tenant traffic (region-us-west, model-recommender) using two key-shaping strategies: conservative mask (mask numeric tokens) and pattern collapse (reduce UUID-like tokens to one token). Simulated TTL ladders predicted cost reductions of 12%-16% for top-10% hot prefixes and neutral-to-positive effect on tail latency. Offline A/B shadowing for 48h showed hit-rate uplift of ~9% on hot cohorts and no measurable 95th-pct latency increase. Risk observed: for ~0.6% of prefixes, key-shape combos introduced unexpected prefix collisions; mitigated by adding collision lookups and per-prefix opt-out.
rollout_plan: - Phase 0: Instrumentation and small-scale shadowing (complete) - Phase 1: Canary apply to internal workloads (1% of production) with 6-hour burn-in and automated checks (scheduled) - Phase 2: Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% over 7 days, each step validated for 6 hours - Phase 3: Full apply with weekly review and periodic re-evaluation - Safety: automatic rollback on any of: (a) P95 latency increase > 7% for affected routes, (b) token cost increase > 5% relative to baseline, (c) hit-rate drop > 6% for >10 prefixes aggregated, or (d) any customer-facing error rate increase > 0.05%.
safety_and_rollback_details: Rollback fences implemented as configuration flags: change-id can be paused and reverted via API. Each change deployed with shadow logs and a rollback window. In addition to automated triggers, runbook step-by-step rollback instructions are linked. We will keep a 48-hour warm-retention of pre-change snapshots for quick rehydration. For key-shaping collisions, implement immediate opt-out per prefix and a monitored reconciliation job that redistributes affected entries.
open_questions: What is acceptable per-customer variance for cost changes (should large enterprise customers be excluded by default)?
Do we expose an admin UI for prefix opt-out or keep it request-level annotation only?
Should we timebox key-shape heuristics experimentation before promoting to global defaults?
notes: - Security review requested for potential user-identifying token masks; applying strict masking rules first. - Observability changes include per-prefix histograms and a new rollout status panel. - Cost model uses latest unit prices from pricing-service v2.
